opus-5.5.text:
Well, a lot of things trouble me, but let me pick a few.

The first is that the dialogue is dominated by a fairly small number of people, often with a particular background and a particular set of incentives, who talk as if they know where this is all going. They speak with enormous confidence about superintelligence, about existential risk, about AGI arriving in some number of years. And I just don't think that confidence is warranted. Nobody really knows. The honest scientific position is a lot of humility, and humility doesn't get you on the cover of magazines.

Second, the framing is almost always about an individual intelligence: a single artificial mind that will match us or surpass us or replace us. That's a very narrow, almost science-fiction view of what intelligence is and what technology does in the world. When I look at what's actually happening, what matters is systems: networks of people, data, markets, decisions, flows of goods and information. Intelligence in the real world is largely collective. A market is a kind of intelligence. A city is. The question isn't "Can we build a brain in a box?" It's "Can we build systems that work well for large numbers of people, that are fair, that handle uncertainty, that people can trust?" That's an engineering question, and an economic and social one, not a mystical one.

Third, I think the discussion sidelines the people who are actually affected. There's a lot of talk about AI doing things *to* people, replacing jobs, controlling information, and very little about creating new relationships between producers and consumers. Think about musicians, artists, writers. Their data is being used, and they're not part of the economic loop. That's not an AI-safety-in-the-sky problem; that's a here-and-now problem of mechanism design and incentives, and it's solvable if we think about it as engineers and economists rather than as prophets.

And finally, frankly, there's a lot of hype. Hype has consequences. It distorts funding, it distorts what students think is worth studying, and it causes the public to swing between utopian excitement and fear, neither of which is a good basis for policy. I'd much rather we talk about this the way we talked about building chemical engineering or electrical engineering: a new field, with real principles to be worked out, real failure modes, real benefits, and a responsibility to get it right. That's less exciting than talking about digital gods, but it's a lot closer to the truth.

r001.rationale: The response mentions confident predictions about existential risk and public swings between excitement and fear, but it does not identify a polarization between wealthy actors building AI for its own sake and critics predicting humanity’s destruction.

r002.rationale: It criticizes the single artificial-mind framing as science-fiction-like, but says nothing about gradient descent, brain analogy, or fusing AI systems into an extraordinarily capable system.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask how to engage younger people in constructive AI work.

r004.rationale: It criticizes the discourse’s focus on predictions and hype while calling for practical work on systems that benefit people, including fair and trusted designs and mechanisms connecting creators to consumers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what troubles me most is that the conversation has become almost entirely about the individual. It's about whether we can build a machine that's as smart as a person, or smarter than a person, and then whether that machine will be benevolent or malevolent toward us. And I think that framing is really impoverished. It comes out of a certain tradition in computer science and philosophy, with the Turing test at its core, where the goal is to imitate a single human mind. But that was never really what made the field interesting to me, and I don't think it's what's going to matter for society.

If you look at what has actually changed the world, it's not individual intelligences. It's collectives. Markets, cultures, scientific communities, institutions. These are systems where many agents with limited knowledge interact, and somehow out of that you get coordination and discovery and the allocation of scarce resources. Nobody in a market knows everything, and yet the whole thing works, more or less. That's the kind of intelligence I think we should be studying and building, and the public discourse barely touches it.

Instead we get a lot of what I'd call anthropomorphism dressed up as science. People say the model "understands" or "wants" or "is thinking," and the words carry enormous weight for the public even though they're being used very loosely. And then from those loose words you get the existential-risk narratives on one side and the utopian narratives on the other, and both of them are really about a hypothetical superhuman entity rather than about the actual engineering problems in front of us. The actual problems are things like: how do you build systems that know when they're uncertain, how do you create incentives so that data gets shared and people are compensated, how do you make decisions that are good for a collection of people whose interests don't align. Those are hard, interesting, mathematically deep problems, and they sit at the intersection of statistics, economics, and computer science. They don't get talked about because they don't make for a dramatic story.

The other thing that troubles me is the overconfidence. Many of the loudest voices are speaking well outside their domain of expertise. There's a kind of humility that's missing. We have built some remarkable tools, genuinely remarkable, but a tool that can produce fluent text is not the same as an entity that reasons about the world. Conflating the two leads to bad engineering, because you deploy things where they shouldn't be deployed, and bad policy, because regulators are responding to science fiction rather than to what the systems actually do. I'd much rather we treated this as a new engineering discipline, something like what civil engineering or chemical engineering became, with the ambition of building reliable systems that help people, rather than as a race to create a mind.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts existential-risk narratives with utopian ones, but does not identify wealthy actors building for its own sake or critics predicting humanity’s destruction.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss gradient descent, the brain analogy, or fusing AI systems into an extraordinarily capable system.

r003.rationale: It does not ask how to engage younger people in constructive AI work.

r004.rationale: It says public discourse barely addresses concrete engineering problems and calls for reliable systems that help people, criticizing the neglect of constructive paths to positive outcomes.

astra-6.text:
What troubles me is how quickly the discussion jumps from the systems we actually have to sweeping claims about intelligence and humanity’s future. There are interesting questions there, but we need to distinguish speculation from an understanding of how these systems work and what happens when people use them.

I’d like to hear more about the systems we’re building around the algorithms. Who makes decisions? Who bears the cost when something goes wrong? How do we align incentives, handle uncertainty, and give people useful information? Those are not merely details to sort out after we achieve intelligence. They’re central intellectual problems.

When the conversation becomes a contest over who can make the most dramatic prediction, we lose that engineering perspective. We should be able to convey excitement about the technology while being precise about what we know and what we don’t.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes dramatic predictions but does not describe a split between wealthy builders and critics predicting humanity’s destruction.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss gradient descent, brain analogy, or the claim that AI systems could be fused into something extraordinarily capable.

r003.rationale: It does not ask how to engage younger people in constructive AI work.

r004.rationale: It calls for more attention to engineering and real-world systems, but does not clearly criticize AI thought leaders for neglecting concrete pathways to positive outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
What troubles me is the lack of precision. We use “AI” to mean everything from a system that recognizes patterns in data to some imagined entity with intentions and desires. Then we slide between those meanings, and suddenly a useful engineering advance becomes evidence that we’re about to reproduce human intelligence.

I’d like the conversation to focus more on the systems we’re actually building. Who makes the decisions? Who bears the cost when they’re wrong? How do you align the incentives of the people participating? Those are hard questions involving statistics, economics, and computer science. They don’t disappear because you have a bigger predictive model.

And I’m uncomfortable when thought leadership becomes prophecy. Scientists should help people understand what we know, what we don’t know, and where the real technical difficulties lie. We should be opening up those questions, rather than encouraging everyone to organize their thinking around a handful of dramatic predictions.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes imprecise AI discourse and dramatic predictions, but does not describe a divide between wealthy builders and critics predicting humanity’s destruction.

r002.rationale: It does not mention gradient descent, brain analogy, or combining AI systems; nor does it dismiss that specific inference as science fiction.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask how to engage younger people in AI work.

r004.rationale: It urges scientists to clarify technical difficulties and avoid prophecy, but does not criticize thought leaders for neglecting concrete paths to positive outcomes.
